It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. entry.title: San José State President Enlisted Harry Edwards To Sabotage Students’ Pro-Palestine Encampment
entry.summary: As heartening as it was to see the wave of student-led Gaza solidarity encampments across college campuses in the spring of 2024, it was just as appalling to see the crackdowns from those same schools' administrations. Across the world, university leaders showed that they were willing to sacrifice the safety of their own students and faculty, rather than divest from any companies that had financial ties to a state committing active genocide. The most closely covered protest was at Columbia University, where the school ultimately sent in the NYPD to dismantle the camp and assault students. The response dragged on for months; a WhatsApp group strategized on how to get the protestors deported, and put together a list of targets. Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil is currently appealing a deportation order, after he was held in ICE detention without criminal charges for over 100 days. On the other side of the country in 2024, UCLA's security and local police stood by as masked goons attacked students within the Gaza solidarity encampment, and tossed fireworks at them. Roughly 30 of the students and faculty attacked have sued UCLA for civil rights violations. Because of reporting last week from Bradford William Davis and Kaya Henkes-Power at the publication Eyeblack, another school administration's grimy efforts have come to light, two years later. When San José State University students put together their Gaza solidarity encampment in 2024, they convened at the Victory Salute statue, a monument on campus honoring the school's alumni Tommie Smith and John Carlos for their raised fists at the 1968 Summer Olympics. The statue was created in 2005 by the Portuguese artist Ricardo Gouveia, who goes by the moniker Rigo 23.

entry.title: Irreal: Integrating Frames Into Your Workflow
entry.summary:
nice post on how he uses frames in his workflow. The TL;DR is that because he often works on several projects in parallel, he has a separate frame for each project. That makes a lot of sense. You don’t get buffers confused among projects and everything for a project is “in one place”.
That brings up the problem of switching among frames. There is, of course, other-frame (Ctrl+x 5 o) but like other-window it can be a bit clunky. Mbork set out to remedy that by writing a function to switch to a given named frame. That’s sort of like ace-window for frames, except that you use the frame name instead of a label generated on the fly.
The first problem is that frame names don’t have to be unique. It wouldn’t be too hard to enforce unique names manually but mbork decided to rewrite set-frame-name to enforce a unique name when naming a frame. It’s pretty simple and should probably be the Emacs default.
Once he had a way of ensuring unique frame names, he rewrote select-frame-by-name to select a frame by name and to create a frame with that name if one doesn’t already exist. The result is a very nice workflow for handling several projects that you’re working on at the same time. Take a look at mbork’s post for the details.

entry.title: It’s Never Too Late To Be The Best Band In The World Again
entry.summary: We begin at Webster Hall in New York City. I'm standing on the main floor with the rest of the general admission patrons. My best friend Howard is with me. He's been waiting nearly as many years as I have for what's about to transpire. So has everyone else in the room. Many of them are already drunk. Many more are still queued up in the line at the merch stand, which has run out of at least one line of T-shirts and will likely run out of others. Howard and I are soaking in the pre-concert playlist playing over the loudspeakers, and waiting for the lights to go dark. I've put in my earplugs. I can't hear anything Howard says, but it doesn't matter. He's ready. I'm ready. Everyone is ready, because we're about to witness the resurrection of Sugar, one of the greatest bands of the 1990s. None of us believed this band would reunite. Never considered the possibility, really. Shit, prior to tonight I didn't even think the members of Sugar—guitarist/vocalist Bob Mould, bassist David Barbe, drummer Malcolm Travis—had considered the idea themselves. For Mould, the ringleader, Sugar wasn't even the most famous band he'd played in. The fact that they're here together on this opening night of the "Love You Even Still" tour, and that we're all here to witness it, feels like a happy fluke. But this is no fluke at all. This is a reunion that required many years, plus a well-timed video birthday card, to become a reality. I have seen Mould on his own in concert more times than I can count, but I've never seen him take the stage live with Travis and Barbe. That's because I discovered Sugar's music a beat too late. They had already broken up before my roommate put on their second album, File Under: Easy Listening, in our college dorm room. Once I heard the opening chords to "Gee Angel," I knew right away that Sugar was my band. That they would always be my band. If I never got to see them in the flesh, so be it. The music had me forever. I knew it back in 1997, and I still know it today, 29 years later.

entry.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: A grid display for Emacs image triage
entry.summary:
A couple days ago I started typing a new Emacs mode for really fast image viewing and triage. (Click the link to read the rationale behind all this.) But after working with it for some hours, I realised that the layout just wasn’t ideal:
If we’re doing a line based layout, you have to have really small thumbnails — otherwise you get so little information density in a screenful. And then I realised that the file names have very little interest. The size is only interesting if it’s zero — that’s a broken image, but a missing thumbnail would also tell me that. The date is the most interesting thing, but since I’m sorting by date, it’s not that vital anyway. So:
A grid! Well, duh. The package can do both layouts, but defaults to using a grid now. The image details are still available, both as tooltips, via a command, and shown automatically when walking through the images with TAB:
I think that’s kinda usable? Gives you an overview while tabbing through images. Fast. Vroom vroom. You can find the code on Microsoft Github.

entry.title: Irreal: Moving Among Windows
entry.summary:
Ray on Emacs, Ray Zeitler writes about moving among windows . It was a nostalgic moment for me because other-window Ctrl+x o) is that you may have to invoke it several times and, as Zeitler says, you can easily overshoot your target.
The next step in my journey—and apparently in Zeitler’s—was the discovery of Windmove. It allows you to use the arrow keys with (by default) the Shift key to move through the windows in a two-dimensional way. It’s a big improvement over the standard other-window command but it does interfere with certain Org bindings.
The next step in my journey was the discovery of abo-abo’s excellent ace-window package. It allows you to easily move among windows as well as perform many other actions such as splitting, deleting, moving, and copying windows. You can see a complete list at the link. To be honest, I use it almost exclusively for changing focus to another window. It works just like abo-abo’s other ace functions. You invoke it (I use Ctrl+x o to leverage my muscle memory) and the windows are labeled. Then you merely choose the label of the window to want to move to. As as added feature, if there are only two windows, it simply moves to the other window without the need for further input. You can also precede the command with the universal argument and it will swap the windows instead of simply moving to the target window.
All-in-all, ace-window is the best package I’ve found for window control. Perhaps it will be the next step on Zeitler’s journey too.

entry.title: Raymond Zeitler: Emacs Windows Management With windmove
entry.summary:
0
Recently I came across the windmove functions1. This discovery caused me to lose interest in bookmarks; now bookmarks are a mere curiosity.
The windmove functions allow you to "operate" on a window; the target window is given as a direction relative to point. Operations include:
selection, like next-window, but direction overrides window order deletion, like delete-window, but direction indicates the window to delete buffer display (not yet in use by the author) S-<left>, S-<right>, S-<up>, S-<down> for window selection. For example, you can activate the window on the left with windmove-left or S-<left>.
Org users already press S-<left> (and S-<right>) on a heading to change TODO status. As well, we press S-<up> (and S-<down>) to increase (decrease) a heading's priority. Luckily, it's easy to specify a different modifier key. I configured my system to make windmove-dir respond to M-s-<dir>2 with the following statement:
(windmove-default-keybindings '(meta super))
windmove-delete-left. I've defined C-M-s-<dir>3 for the windmove-delete-dir functions by adding this to my init file:
(windmove-delete-default-keybindings '(control meta super))
other-window (C-x o), sometimes "overshooting" the desired window, or I'd resort to using the mouse to click in it. Now with this intuitive method of selecting windows, I can keep my hands on the keyboard and spend less time figuring out how to get around.
Try it out!
0 See: https://ray-on-emacs.blogspot.com/2026/11/emacs-carnival-november-2026.html
1 Emacs windmove help page
2 On Windows, I hold down the Alt and Win keys while pressing an arrow key.
3 As above, but additionally with the Control key. It's surprisingly easy, in fact.

entry.title: Irreal: Manual Dired Search
entry.summary:
The Art Of Not Asking Why reminds us of a very useful technique for iteratively searching through a series of files for those that contain a given set of terms. The process if simple but very flexible:
Open a Dired buffer with the files you want to search. Use %g to do a regular expression search through the files for one of the terms. The files containing the term will be marked. Use t to toggle the marks, resulting in all the files that don’t contain the term being marked. Use k to temporarily hide the marked files, leaving only those that contain the term. Go to step 2 using the next term. A command to search through the contents of the marked files and show the results in another buffer.
The nice thing about this method is that it’s interactive: you progressively narrow down the list of target files by eliminating files that don’t contain the terms your looking for. You can, as JTR says, even manually eliminate files that you don’t want to consider as you go along. It’s a good technique and worth remembering.

entry.title: Irreal: Opening Techinfo Sourced Web Pages In Emacs
entry.summary:
interesting little utility. Although it’s restricted to Safari and the Mac, it’s a nice idea that could probably be ported to other operating systems without difficulty. The idea is to be able to easily move from reading a Web page generated by Techinfo to reading the same information with the Emacs Info reader.
Reading Info pages with Emacs is straightforward and comfortable but the external utilities to read them outside of Emacs are terrible. Therefore, a lot us who started with another editor learned to go to the Web first rather than try to navigate the horrible external reader packages. But, as Choi points out, recent events have shown us that we can’t always count on the Web being there for us.
Choi’s solution to all this is the Counterpart utility that provides a menu in Safari to open the Web page’s content in Emacs. Of course, this only works for Techinfo generated content. Your immediate reaction may be, “Who cares?” but I’ve sometimes wished for something like this so that I could have the content side by side with whatever I was working on in Emacs. That also make’s it easy to copy text out of the Info buffer when you want to add a quote to whatever you’re writing.

entry.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: Herp derp I eat paste
entry.summary:
A year and a half ago I made a kitchen clock, which has worked well (except that I had to swap out the screen which broke mysteriously). But yesterday I was having some work done here, so I had to remove one of the wifi access points here, and… the clock stopped working. *gasp* Yes, because I had in my infinite wisdom decided that I would generate the clock face on a different machine, because the clock is a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and I just assumed that it didn’t have enough memory to run Emacs (which I am, being a totally rational person, using to generate the SVG that’s being displayed). So it’s a Rube Goldberguesque setup of having the image being generated on the main server, and then scp‘d over once a minute, and then being displayed on the console here in the kitchen. But the wifi outage made me wonder — is it true that the machine doesn’t have enough memory to do it all on device?
So it’s got 416MB of useful memory, and while just running and doing nothing special, it’s using 129MB of that. What happens if I load an Emacs with all the SVG libraries and stuff and generate the image?
It’s using 186MB — so the Emacs occupies about 50MB max. *sigh* It’s so easy to think of Emacs as this “big thing”, but everything has gotten so much bigger around it that it doesn’t matter at all any more. So now I’ve changed the code to run on-device, so the only thing that goes AWOL if the wifi goes missing is updated temperatures.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Opening Texinfo Web Pages in Emacs Info
entry.summary: As convenient as accessing online services can be, any disruption in availability without a fallback is painful. Given events of late, many are learning the hard way what it’s like to live without that fallback. GNU Emacs has long supported reading documentation via the Info reader package. Info reader is a “local first” system, where all documentation is stored locally. The source format of the documentation is Texinfo which is exported to different formats, among them Info (used by the Emacs Info reader), HTML, and PDF. Texinfo exported HTML is typically hosted on a website (usually GNU Project), with each Info node mapped to a URL path and indexed by most major search engine services. Discovery of information in Texinfo documentation is frequently done via web search. If the user desires to view that Texinfo web page in the Emacs Info reader, that has to be done manually by corresponding the web page to its Info node. Counterpart is a new utility to automate opening the Info node counterpart of a Texinfo exported web page in Emacs. This utility is designed for Emacs users on macOS who also use the Safari web browser. It requires the installation of a macOS Shortcut which is run from the main menu bar. More detail on using it can be found in the Counterpart User Guide. Once a desired Info node is opened in Emacs, you can then bookmark it for later access, no internet connection required.

entry.summary:
huge fan of Journelly, which I use many times a day as my memo book. It has many other uses so take a look at the link if you’re interested in a note taking/journaling/private tweet/memo book application. I can’t recommend it enough.
Ramírez has, of course, done many other things, many or perhaps most, in the Emacs sphere. See his site for details. In a recent post he writes about making contributions to Emacs and getting them merged. Those of you who have been down that road know that it’s hard to get started. You have to navigate the GNU copyright assignment process, which seems needlessly baroque until you remember that all this is being run by volunteers.
You can follow the link to find out what his contributions are. They are all live in Emacs 31 so if you are up to date they are available to you now. The main takeaway for me was the satisfaction that Ramírez got from making those contributions. None of them were huge changes and merely scratched an itch that Ramírez had. If you have a small itch that you’ve scratched, you should consider sharing it with the community. You too can become part of Emacs’ long and influential history just as Hari Seldon’s successors in the Second Foundation contributed their own additions to Seldon’s Psychohistory.

entry.summary: Last year I improved my code for copying the current location to the kill ring. Recently it occurred to me that this was not the last word. In fact, I’m pretty surprised I didn’t think of it earlier – it’s sort of obvious in hindsight. The idea is that it should copy the range of lines when the region is active.
